title: Depping 2018 dissertation (Univ. Saskatchewan), Manuscript B = Depping & Mandryk CHI PLAY 2017 'Cooperation and Interdependence: How Multiplayer Games Increase Social Closeness'
label: research
claim: 2x2 between-subjects online experiment (cooperative vs competitive x interdependent vs independent roles) in a two-player puzzle game, voice chat, MTurk, 138 recruited, F-tests with df 1,101. Cooperation raised in-game relatedness (eta2 .07), enjoyment (.05), invested effort (.06), trust (.11); interdependence raised relatedness (.04), enjoyment (.08), trust (.12) but not effort. No cooperation x interdependence interaction on relatedness, enjoyment or trust, i.e. the two effects add rather than amplify. Competence, autonomy, intuitive controls unaffected. Tension: interaction (eta2 .05), interdependence lowered tension when competing and raised it when cooperating. Stranger pairs, 10 minutes of play, MTurk sample; short-term social closeness only. Dissertation also reports a field study where interdependence AND toxicity predicted in-game social capital, and in-game social capital was negatively associated with loneliness (read in abstract only).

title: Ryan, Rigby & Przybylski 2006, The motivational pull of video games: an SDT approach (Motivation and Emotion 30:347-363), Study 4
label: research
claim: Study 4: survey of 730 members (679 male, 51 female, mean age 22.1) of an online gaming community with MMO experience, recruited via a forum with a raffle. Cross-sectional, self-report. In-game relatedness (PENS) independently predicted game enjoyment and intended future play along with autonomy and competence; for hours per week, competence and relatedness (and Yee's achievement motive) had unique variance. Yee's achievement/competitive motive predicted LOWER post-play mood but MORE hours per week; authors read this as competitive tendency bringing pressure and stress. Relatedness correlated r=.66 with Yee's social motive. Sample is heavily male and self-selected; correlational, no causal claim possible.

title: Johannes, Vuorre & Przybylski 2021, Video game play is positively correlated with well-being (Royal Society Open Science)
label: research
claim: Telemetry from EA (Plants vs Zombies: Battle for Neighborville, 518 survey completers) and Nintendo (Animal Crossing: New Horizons, 6,011 respondents; 2,756 with two-week telemetry). Objective two-week playtime to well-being (SPANE): beta .10 [.02,.18] PvZ and .06 [.03,.09] AC:NH, R2 = .01 each. Authors estimate roughly 80 hours of play over two weeks for a half-SD change in AC:NH. Need satisfaction (autonomy, relatedness, extrinsic motivation significant in both games) predicted well-being; playtime was not significant once motivation was in the model. Relatedness was asked only of players who played with others and predicted well-being positively; study does NOT compare social vs solo play. Cross-sectional, response rates 0.21% and 1.75%, COVID period, no preregistration, only two games. I read the first 100,000 of 110,277 characters.

title: Vuorre, Johannes, Magnusson & Przybylski 2022, Time spent playing video games is unlikely to impact well-being (Royal Society Open Science)
label: research
claim: Three-wave panel over about six weeks, 38,935 active players (from 108,880 consented) across seven games (Animal Crossing NH, Apex Legends, Eve Online, Forza Horizon 4, Gran Turismo Sport, Outriders, The Crew 2); logs from publishers. Cross-lagged model; play time to affect: per extra hour/day interval (-0.09, 0.16) on a 13-point scale; to life satisfaction -0.04 (-0.15, 0.09). Authors: effects 'probably very small'; intrinsic motivation related to life satisfaction (0.18 [0.08,0.32]) more than quantity of play. Social or multiplayer play NOT analysed as a factor. Limits: response rates 0.1-3.0%, attrition, causal estimate changed direction under some missing-not-at-random scenarios, only total play time measured, not preregistered. Read via a fetch summariser, not raw text.

title: Kwak, Blackburn & Han, CHI 2015, Exploring cyberbullying and other toxic behavior in team competition online games (League of Legends)
label: research
claim: Dataset: over 10 million player reports on 1.46 million toxic players with Tribunal decisions (collected April 2013 from NA, EUW, KR). Reports for accused players skew to the LOSING side: winning ratio clearly below 50% for all report categories despite Elo-style matchmaking, under 15% for intentional feeding and assisting the enemy. Explicit 'report' requests in all-chat raised opponents' reporting odds 16.37 times (chi2(1, N=580,480)=194552.9), so the bystander effect is overcome by an explicit request. Pardon rates: 80.9-86.0% punished per region overall; highest category-level pardon 26.1% (spamming, KR); cyberbullying reports pardoned 17.1% KR, 14.3% NA, 9.7% EUW. Authors conclude voluntary reporting participation is low. Observational; Tribunal reviewers are experienced players, not ground truth; one game, 2013 data. Read via pdftotext, partial (grepped sections plus conclusion).

title: GDC 2013 Riot experimentally investigates online toxicity (Jeffrey Lin talk, written up by Jim Cummings)
label: developer
claim: Secondhand write-up of the talk. Making cross-team chat optional measurably decreased toxicity measures (no percentages in this article); 46-47% of games had no chat before and after. Tribunal: 105 million votes, 280,000 reformed players, community verdicts about 80% agreement with Riot's in-house team (which was more severe). 'Optimus' priming experiment, 5x3x4 factorial: red negative-behaviour stats on the loading screen reduced toxicity more than white; blue positive messages helped; red 'Who will be the most sportsmanlike?' INCREASED all toxicity metrics. No effect sizes in the article. Riot is reporting on its own game, no independent data.

title: Search-result summary of Lin figures on reform cards and chat (MIT Technology Review, Gamasutra and others)
label: snippet
claim: Search-aggregated figures: cross-chat opt-out default gave a 32.7% fall in negative chat in a week; Lin quoted reform rates of 50% with explanation, 65-70% with chat-log evidence, and MIT Tech Review reported 92%; one source says 98% verdict agreement versus the 80% in the Gamasutra write-up. Figures conflict across sources, so none are safe to cite from this reading.

title: Chen, Xue, Kolen, Aghdaie, Zaman, Sun & Seif El-Nasr, WWW 2017, EOMM: An Engagement Optimized Matchmaking Framework (EA)
label: research
claim: Matchmaking posed as a min-weight perfect matching on pairwise churn risk; skill-equal pairing proved a special case under a simplified assumption. Table 1, real EA PvP game: 7-day churn risk after a match is 5.1% for three losses in a row (LLL) versus 2.6-2.7% for states like DLW/LLW/LDW/DDD and 3.7% for WWW. Evaluation is a SIMULATION built on real data (churn model trained on logs, Glicko skill, 20% draws assumed), 10,000 rounds, pool sizes 100-500, retained players in the next eight hours: EOMM 261.19 vs SkillMM 259.24 at P=500; gains over SkillMM 0.3, 0.9, 1.1, 0.6% at P=200-500 (avg 0.7%); at P=100 EOMM did not beat RandomMM significantly and was below SkillMM. The 15% figure is the authors' compounding extrapolation (1.007^20) over 20 rounds, not measured. Not deployed live; 1v1 only; paper itself notes team games need hypergraph matching. Optimises a churn model, so it can deliberately give players losses.

title: Sailer, Hense, Mayr & Mandl 2017, How gamification motivates (Computers in Human Behavior 69:371-380)
label: research
claim: Randomised online simulation (logistics task), 699 logged in, 419 completed, 331 analysed after excluding 88 who failed a treatment check (control n=150; condition 1 badges+leaderboards+performance graphs n=103; condition 2 avatars+story+teammates n=78). Competence: control 3.76 vs condition 1 4.19 (F(2,328)=3.39, p<.05, eta2p=.020). Relatedness: condition 2 1.77 vs control 1.49 vs condition 1 1.45 (F=3.48, eta2p=.032); the leaderboard bundle did NOT raise relatedness, the teammates/avatar/story bundle did. Decision-freedom autonomy unaffected. Effects are small; leaderboard cannot be separated from badges and graphs; relatedness means are low (about 1.5 on the scale used); authors admit the manipulation was recognised by too few players. Short single session.

title: Landers, Bauer & Callan 2017, Gamification of task performance with leaderboards: a goal setting experiment (Computers in Human Behavior 71:508-515)
label: research
claim: Brainstorming task, participants assigned to do-your-best, easy, difficult or impossible goals, with a leaderboard whose scores matched those conditions. The leaderboard produced performance comparable to the difficult and impossible goal conditions, read by the authors as participants implicitly adopting a goal near the top of the board; goal commitment behaved as with assigned goals. So the board works as a goal, and the displayed top score is the goal. Sample size not seen. A secondary write-up (snippet) says people who did not buy into the leaderboard did worse than those given impossible goals.

title: Mekler, Bruhlmann, Tuch & Opwis 2017, effects of individual gamification elements on intrinsic motivation and performance (CHB 71:525-534), via search records
label: snippet

title: Bisberg, Jiang, Zeng, Chen & Ferrara, CSCW 2022, The Gift That Keeps on Giving: Generosity is Contagious in Multiplayer Online Games (Sky: Children of Light)
label: research
claim: Observational log analysis of Sky. Abstract: players are more engaged after playing with others, especially friends; players who receive or observe generosity become more generous later; both receiving and observing generosity are linked to higher future engagement. Page gave no sample size or effect sizes. Observational, one game, in-game gifting, co-present play; correlational, selection of friendly players into receiving is not ruled out.
